stem: An environmental agency identifies 200 patients with a lifetime history of panic attacks and 200 matched controls without the condition. Exposure to loud traffic noises was compared in two groups. 20 patients and ten controls had such an exposure. Which of the following is false with respect to the above study design?
options: Both exposure and disease have occurred before the onset of the study.
It is less cost effective than following up those who were exposed to loud noise till they have panic attacks
It is mostly useful to study outcomes which are rare
It is mostly useful in diseases where exposure is common
correctAnswer: It is less cost effective than following up those who were exposed to loud noise till they have panic attacks
explanation: The above is an example of case-control study design. The exposure and the outcome have both taken place when the subjects are recruited. It is retrospective, cheap compared to cohort studies and is useful to study common exposures (but relatively rare outcomes).

stem: In a case-control study of possible nutritional correlates of depression, subjects were asked about the frequency of consuming 20 different food items in a Likert scale. The histories of cases differed significantly from those of controls, at p=.05, for three of the 20 listed items. Which of the following is most likely?
options: The study is inconclusive: further case control studies with more rigorous methods are required
Diet is related to depression; but it is unclear which of the three items is the most important culprit
Diet is not related to depression as the results are due to chance finding: discard the study
The results are conclusive if it could be shown that there was no recall bias
Diet is definitely related to depression; further cohort studies for each of the 3 items are warranted
correctAnswer: The study is inconclusive: further case control studies with more rigorous methods are required
explanation: There are two important problems with this study. Asking depressed subjects to recall numerous food items can produce serious recall bias. In addition, at a significance level of 0.05, at least one out of the 20 items may show an association by chance. As it is difficult to say which of  the three items are really associated with depression, it may not be wise to invest huge effort and money in a cohort study at this stage. It is best if a more rigorous case-control study is attempted to replicate or refute the findings.

stem: A case-control study investigating various risk factors for a disease in hospitalised patients chooses healthy relatives of the patients as controls. In which of the following situations the results may be distorted?
options: Risk factor is related to diet and lifestyle
Risk factor is purely related to occupational exposure
Disease is not shared by families
Exposure is likely to be not shared by families
Risk factor is not related to household environment
correctAnswer: Risk factor is related to diet and lifestyle
explanation: This matching approach increases the likelihood that the factors that are generally shared by family members will be similar for both the controls and the cases. This reduces bias and confounding especially if the cause of a disease is not shared in families. Unfortunately in cases where the causal agent is genetic or otherwise familial, this method leads to "overmatching" thus reducing the ability to demonstrate  the causation.

stem: Which one of the following types of bias is NOT a major concern in a hospital-based case-control study?
explanation: Work up bias (verification bias) refers to a systematic error in the assessment of the validity of a diagnostic test. When the execution of the gold standard is influenced by the results of the assessed test, especially when the reference test is less frequently performed when the assessed test result is negative, then this will influence the number of false negatives correctly identified in the exercise. This bias is specific to assessment of diagnostic tests and so not seen in ordinary case-control studies where cases and controls are determined before  estimates of exposure begin. Family aggregation bias is a type of information bias wherein presence of a case in the family increases awareness of risk factors and exposure leading to more family members of cases reporting an exposure though controls have family members with less awareness. Journal Epid Comm Health 2004;58;635-641

stem: Which of the following describes the relationship between prevalence and incidence rates?
explanation: In a steady-state situation, in which the rates are not changing, and in-migration equals out-migration, the following equation applies - Prevalence = Incidence × Duration of disease. Gordis, L. Epidemiology 4th ed. Chapter 3 Saunders Elsevier

stem: In a study examining the relationship between domestic abuse and depression, women who do and do not suffer abuse are followed up over a five-year period. It is found that 70 of the 500 individuals who undergo domestic abuse develop depression; 150 of 3000 individuals who don't get abused develop depression. If the prevalence of domestic abuse in a particular council is 20%, the expected incidence of depression in this council is
explanation: It = (Prevalence in the exposed)(Incidence in the exposed) + (1-Prevalence in the exposed)(Incidence in the non-exposed) = (20%)(70/500) +  (1-20%)(150/3000) = 0.068 or 6.8%

stem: Cohort studies allow researchers to calculate relative risk and attributable risk. Which of the following statements regarding these measures is true?
options: Attributable risk is a cross product
Attributable risk cannot take negative values
Relative risk cannot take negative values
Attributable risk but not relative risk explains the reason for differences between groups
correctAnswer: Relative risk cannot take negative values
explanation: Relative risk is a ratio - it can have values less than 1, but not less than 0. Attributable risk is an absolute risk difference it can be less than zero when the risk in exposed is less than the risk in non-exposed. Both attributable risk and relative risk are measures of differences between groups - while the former is an absolute difference, the latter is a ratio. The odds ratio is a cross product. 

stem: National Comorbidity Survey examined a possible association between traits of neuroticism and various psychiatric disorders. Trained non- clinical staff screened randomly chosen individuals using well-validated questionnaires to establish lifetime diagnoses in addition to collecting data on drug use, alcohol intake and various personality traits. Which of the following measure of disease occurrence can be calculated from this study?
explanation: Cross-sectional surveys can estimate prevalence only; to find out incidence rates a cohort study or repeated cross-sectional surveys at two  time points is necessary.

stem: A study looks into patient records for a group of schizophrenic patients admitted to a psychiatric hospital between 1934 and 1944. All of the patients were deceased at the time of study. Each patient's social history recorded at the time of admission was scored by two independent raters for the quality of social resources. The impact of social support on the longevity of schizophrenia patients was examined. This study can be described as
explanation: This study involved retrospective data collection. The groups were separated according to the level of social input at the time of admission  (exposure) and then the longevity of life (outcome - which occurred later) was examined. This is a retrospective cohort design. /www.psychosomaticmedicine.org/cgi/content/full/61/2/146

stem: Which of the following study designs is useful to measure point prevalence of a clinical problem?
explanation: A cross-section survey assesses the status of an individual with respect to the presence or absence of a disease at a given point in time. It can be used to assess point prevalence.

stem: Which of the following study designs is useful to measure the incidence of a clinical problem?
explanation: Incidence is defined by number of new cases. One needs to observe a population long enough to pick all new cases. This is achieved by cohort studies.

stem: Which of the following is an advantage of case-control design over cohort design?
options: Can be used to determine survival rates
Can be used to study prodromal course of a disease
Can explore multiple risk factors for the same disease
correctAnswer: Can explore multiple risk factors for the same disease
explanation: Case-control studies are cheaper and faster, compared with other analytic designs. They are useful for studying diseases with long latent periods. They are useful for studying rare diseases since subjects are selected on the basis of disease status. They allow the investigation of multiple exposures simultaneously 

stem: Which of the following study design is suitable for survival analysis?
explanation: Survival data measure follow-up time from a defined starting point to the occurrence of a given event, for example the time from the beginning to the end of a remission period or the time from the diagnosis of a disease to death. Such observations are made possible only by studies using follow-up data (mostly prospective, sometimes retrospective) such as cohort studies. It is also possible in parallel RCT designs but usually not attempted in cross over studies where the observation periods are fairly short (retrieved from  http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1065034/).

stem: A psychology trainee administers Beck's depression inventory to detect unidentified depression among the general population. She enrols subjects for her study by interviewing people who attend the local sports centre and gymnasium. Which of the following bias is most likely?
explanation: It is likely that people who have an active lifestyle by attending leisure centres and gymnasium differ from the general population that has a mixture of active and inactive people. Studying unidentified depression by using a select sample as this will lead to selection bias. 

stem: Two-stage screening surveys are commonly used to estimate the prevalence of psychiatric disorders in the community. In the first stage, questionnaires are sent to a large sample of subjects. The results from this stage are scored and used to identify probable cases who are then clinically interviewed. Which of the following is most likely to obscure true prevalence rates in such studies?
explanation: Selection bias occurs when study participants are selected in such a way that the association between exposure and disease differs for those who participate and those who do not participate in the study. One type of selection bias seen especially in postal surveys is non-response  bias where responders who send their answers back to the researcher systematically differ from non-responders. It is well established that for lifestyle and behaviour related issues, non-responders often tend to have more problems than responders. This applies to mental health issues as well.

stem: A regional affective disorders unit decides to find out patients' satisfaction with their service. They send out an easy-to-use one-page questionnaire to all service users on their list. A specialist trainee collates the results to present as a poster. She reports 85% satisfaction of service users with a questionnaire return rate of 65%. Which of the following is correct?
options: The result is most likely to be an under-estimation of the satisfaction
Satisfaction is a normally distributed variable
Random selection of patients to post questionnaires will be more representative
Systematic differences exist between responders and non-responders
Reminders do not increase reponse rates of postal surveys
correctAnswer:
Systematic differences exist between responders and non-responders


explanation: Satisfaction is not a normally distributed variable. It is likely that the 'most satisfied' group responded while least satisfied group abstained from posting the questionnaire back. This non-response bias could twist the results with an overestimation of actual satisfaction rates.  Sending reminders can increase response rates. But randomly selecting responses that are returned will not provide any respite from non- response bias as the pool from which random selection takes place is in itself biased (i.e. they are all from 'most satisfied people'). Similarly randomly selecting people to send the questionnaire will also be of no use as still the response rate may be low, with non-satisfied people abstaining from returning the questionnaire. www.biomedcentral.com/1472-6963/4/31

stem: A researcher's expectations regarding treatment effect may result in differential interactions with some subjects leading to a change in subject's response in favour of the research hypothesis. This is known as
explanation: The Pygmalion effect is also called the experimenter expectancy effect. Pygmalion is Bernard Shaw's play where a professor bets and succeeds in teaching a poor flower girl to speak and act like a higher-class lady. Mere awareness of the experimenter's expectations regarding treatment effect may result in a change in subject behavior in the direction of experimenter hypothesis. Halo effect refers to a  type of primacy effect in which first impressions or answers influence subsequent answers in a questionnaire or interview. Gray GE. Evidence-based psychiatry. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2004.Pg 57

stem: A clinician involved in a trial could provide additional care to patients in one treatment group but not to those in the other treatment group. This effect is called cointervention bias. This can be reduced by
explanation: A clinician involved in a trial may provide additional care (e.g., time, support, etc.) to patients in one treatment group but not to those in the other treatment group. This effect is known as cointervention or performance bias (Altman et al. 2001). In clinical trials, this effect (and also Pygmalion effect) can be minimized by blinding clinicians to the treatment being provided. Gray GE. Evidence-based psychiatry. American  Psychiatric Publishing, 2004.Pg 57

stem: Both smoking and alcohol consumption are associated with senile cognitive impairment. A study investigating the effect of smoking on dementia fails to stratify exposed group according to drinking index. Which of the following can threaten the validity of conclusions derived from this study?
explanation: A confounder is a factor that is associated both with the exposure of interest and the risk of the disease being studied. Thus, the observed association between the exposure of interest and disease outcome may be incorrect. Confounding causes an error in comparisons between  groups if the groups are not stratified or adjusted.

stem: Despite multiple reminders, a postal survey of heroin users to study disclosure to DVLA had a low response rate. What can be done to improve the interpretation of conclusions from this survey?
options: Repharse the questionnaire and send the new version to nonresponders
Increase sample size by recruting another random group of users
Report the proportion of DVLA-disclosed responders as the lower limit of expected percentage of heroine users who have disclosed to
Ignore non responders and report on the available data
Compare and report the baseline characteristics of responders and non-responders
correctAnswer:
Compare and report the baseline characteristics of responders and non-responders


explanation: It is well established that survey nonresponders are probably different from responders. It is likely that most nonresponders were dissatisfied with the service. Recruiting more people will not simply increase the response rate, and non-responders will probably exist in  equal numbers even in the second random group. The most one can do in this situation is to compare what is known about responders with non-responders. This might throw some light on reasons for nonresponse and help deducting what direction their response might have taken.

stem: Mere observation of behaviour can improve performance. In medical research, this is called
explanation: Hawthorne effect refers to the phenomenon that people participating in a study ('under observation') may improve their performance or behaviour simply because of the attention they receive. This does not occur for physiological parameters such as blood pressure but seen in psychological factors such as motivation, productivity and most measures of self-report. The name derives from a factory called the Hawthorne Works where experiments to improve worker productivity were carried out in the Industrial period. Surprisingly most of the  changes (non-specific) made to workers' conditions temporarily improved productivity. See BMJ 2009; 338:b1164

stem: A scandalous tabloid report suggested that Asperger's syndrome may be more common in infants born to mothers who have irregular periods in the year immediately preceding the birth. A medical charity funds a study to investigate this report. 100 mothers of children with Asperger's syndrome were interviewed with respect to their menstrual history. 100 mothers of similar age and gender distributed normal children were also interviewed. Which of the following may invalidate results in this study?
explanation: Recall bias is a type of information bias. It can be due to rumination bias - the presence of disease influences the perception of its causes or  exposure suspicion bias - the search for exposure to the putative cause once being diagnosed. Though it is classically associated with case- control studies, it can also occur in cohort studies (for example, workers who known their exposure to hazardous substances may show a trend to report more the effects related to them), and trials without participants' blinding. Delgado-Rodriguez and Llorca J. Bias. Journal Epid Comm Health 2004;58;635-641

stem: Using five years follow-up data of 200 patients at a local eating disorder service, a researcher is able to trace up to 80% of subjects registered at the service between 1999-2002. The 5-year mortality in this group is no different from an age, socioeconomic class and gender- matched group in same locality obtained from employment registers. She concludes that mortality rates associated with anorexia are overestimated in other studies. Which of the following invalidates such conclusion?
options: Lack of data on physical health
explanation: It is highly likely that the untraced subjects in this study are actually deceased. In mortality studies, attrition bias is a very important concern. 

stem: The percentage of group members having quit smoking at post-test was found much higher in a group having received a quit-smoking training program than in the control group in an RCT. Which of the following must be carefully checked while interpreting the study results?
options: Percentage completing the quit smoking program
correctAnswer:
Percentage completing the quit smoking program

explanation: Recall bias is unlikely in this scenario of a controlled trial; as the measurement pertains to percentage responders, regression towards the mean is also unlikely. But presence of high drop out rates can bias the results as it is likely that those who will not be successful in quitting will drop out of the program earlier than the ones who are more likely to succeed. This is important when considering translating evidence  to clinical practice.

stem: To be called a confounder, the third variable that is suspected to mediate the relationship between a cause and an effect must satisfy which of the following criteria?
options: It must be related to both the cause and the effect
It should be on the causal pathway that is being investigated
It must be consistently present along with the causal event
correctAnswer: It must be related to both the cause and the effect
explanation: A confounder is an extraneous third variable that correlates with both the dependent and independent variables in a study. Restriction, randomization, standardization, stratification and multivariate methods are various ways of eliminating the effect of a confounder. 

stem: Which of the following is not a suitable method to reduce confounders in a study before the data is collected?
explanation: Restriction, randomization, standardization, stratification and multivariate methods are various ways of eliminating the effect of a confounder. Of these multivariate methods such as regression can be used only after data collection, at the stage of analysis.

stem: Which of the following conditions of causality make cohort studies better than case-control studies in exploring causal association?
options: Temporal association between cause and outcome
correctAnswer:
Temporal association between cause and outcome


explanation: The conditions of causality, as proposed by Bradford Hill, include 1. temporal association. 2. dose-response association 3. specificity of association 4. consistency of association 5. plausibility of biological reasoning 6. strength of association. Among this temporal association could not be demonstrated using a case-control design which is retrospective. 

stem: A statistician explains to you that confounders are not eliminated by randomisation. But he still insists randomisation is the best way of controlling confounding bias. Which of the following is a suitable explanation?
options: Statistically checking for confounders is not necessary if adequate randomisation is done
Confounders can cause an effect only if they are distributed differently between study groups
Confounders are identified and restricted by the randomisation process
Confounders can be statistically checked only in randomised samples
correctAnswer:
Confounders can cause an effect only if they are distributed differently between study groups


explanation: Confounders can cause an effect only if they are distributed differently between study groups. This is the principle behind randomisation to reduce confounders. 

stem: A study finds that the risk of developing hyperglycaemia is high in outpatients taking antipsychotics compared to antidepressants. The odds ratio is higher for a subgroup of psychotic patients with family history of diabetes. Family history of diabetes can be considered as
explanation: Research studies tend to analyse the relationship between a cause and effect. A third factor can influence this relationship. This third factor is called a confounder if it distorts the relationship and produces an incorrect result. The confounding factor can disturb the association only if it is distributed unevenly in exposed and unexposed individuals. By contrast, effect modifier is a third factor that affects the magnitude of  the cause-effect relationship. Effect modification provides important information and is not related to unequal distribution. One way of differentiating between confounders and effect modifiers is by studying crude relative risk and stratified relative risk. If crude risk differs from adjusted risk, we can conclude that the stratified factor is a confounder. If the relative risk of one stratum is different from other strata (subgroups) then we can call the factor as an effect modifier. Sometimes, a factor can be both confounder and effect modifier.

stem: Which of the following statistical procedures involve stratified analysis of odds ratio in the presence of confounding?
explanation: The Mantel-Haenszel technique is an excellent method for adjusting for confounding factors when analysing the relationship between a dichotomous outcome and a dichotomous risk factor.

stem: Which of the following methods is NOT used to minimise confounding factors in a case-control study?
explanation: Randomisation, restriction and matching are three methods that can be used while designing a study to control for confounders. Alternatively, we can handle the problem of confounding in the data analysis in one of the two ways: stratification or adjustment.

stem: Various study designs can be used to investigate causality. In such investigations, the most important difference between an experimental study and an observational study is that
options: The researcher controls the exposure of the subjects in an experimental study
The study and control groups are selected according to exposure status in an experimental study
The experimental study needs ethical approval
The study and control groups are carefully matched in an experimental study
correctAnswer:
The researcher controls the exposure of the subjects in an experimental study


explanation: In experimental studies, the exposure of the subjects to a putative causal factor / treatment factor is controlled by the researcher. Both types of studies need ethical approval. Cohort studies are observational and still prospective. Matching two groups is necessary for both types of studies. This can be achieved by randomization in experiments. 

stem: While conducting a study, all enrolled subjects were matched for age, gender, smoking and body mass index before studying to control for confounding. Which of the following type of studies is most suitable for the above method?
options: A cross-sectional study design to study interaction between multiple social and environmental variables on adolescent depression
An ecological study using data from the UK household survey
A prospective cohort study of 1684 subjects.
A case control study requiring a total sample size of 30 each.
A randomised control trial evaluating the effect of Bupropion on smoking cessation.
correctAnswer:
A case control study requiring a total sample size of 30 each.


explanation: Matching is possible for smaller studies. It is not needed for RCTs and extremely difficult for large cohort studies. It is not possible for ecological studies and cross-sectional surveys. 

stem: Which of the following is not a criterion used in assessing the evidence for causality in medical research?
explanation: Hill's criteria for causality includes consistency, specificity, temporality and biological gradient (dose-response relationship). Consistency refers to the association being repeatedly observed in studies performed by different persons, in different settings, among different populations and using different methods. If a specific exposure can be isolated from others and associated with a specific disease, then such specificity supports causality. This is perhaps the most difficult criterion to fulfill because in practice many exposures (e.g., cigarettes or  radiation) are associated with multiple effects and specific diseases often have more than one cause. Temporality refers to time relationship between cause and effect: the factor believed to have caused the disease must have occurred prior to disease development. Hill AB: The environment and disease: Association or causation? Proc R Soc Med 58:295-330, 1965

stem: An observed dose-response effect supports the hypothesis of a causal relationship, according to Hill's criteria. But many well-designed studies of a genuinely causal relationship may fail to show a dose-response effect. Which is the least likely explanation for such results?
options: All doses are too low to reveal the effect
There is no real dose-response effect
All doses are too high to reveal the effect
correctAnswer:
There is no real dose-response effect


explanation: If a dose-response relationship is present, it provides a strong evidence for a causal relationship. However, the absence of a dose-response relationship does not necessarily rule out a causal relationship. In some cases in which a threshold may exist, no disease may develop up to a certain level of exposure; above this threshold level, the disease may manifest. The study might have included only below threshold  exposures; similarly if there is a dose window only within which the response occurs, again this may be missed if all participants are outside the window. Similarly confounders and random variation may obscure the association.

stem: Which of the following methods can be used to evaluate both confounders and effect modifiers in a study examining causal association
explanation: Stratification can help analyse the effect modifiers and confounders in a study.

stem: In a large Finnish cohort study of the relationship between bullying and depression in adult life, the crude relative risk was 5.0. When the data was stratified according to socioeconomic class of parents, the relative risks are 7.0 for the class I, 3.0 for the class II, and 1.5 for the class III and the Mantel-Haenszel adjusted rate was 3. The most appropriate conclusion from the study must be
options: Bullying is associated with three times more risk of depression in adult life; the risk is confounded by socioeconomic status of parents
Bullying is associated with three times more risk of depression in adult life; the risk is modified according to socioeconomic status of
Bullying is associated with 11.5 times more risk of depression in adult life
Bullying is associated with four times (on average across various socioeconomic groups) more risk of depression in adult life
Bullying is associated with 3.8 times more risk of depression in adult life
correctAnswer:
Bullying is associated with three times more risk of depression in adult life; the risk is modified according to socioeconomic status of parents


explanation: As crude rates do not differ from adjusted rates, the socioeconomic status is not a confounder, but as strata differ among each other, it is an  effect modifier. One must use the adjusted rates when giving the final study result - averages or sums are not appropriate.

stem:
Qualitative research A qualitative research study is conducted to obtain the views of patients with schizophrenia regarding the nature of mental health care they received. From the list of options above choose the most appropriate method for proceeding with this study for each question below:

Method used to reach adequate sample size Choose...

You include an independent rater to look at the data collected when analysing it. Choose...

You ask psychologists and social workers who provide care to the participating patients to be the study subjects to achieve a wider perspective Choose...

You want a systematic approach to analyse the data as and when it is collected. Choose...
correctAnswer:
Method used to reach adequate sample size → Theoretical saturation, You include an independent rater to look at the data collected when analysing it. → Triangulation, You ask psychologists and social workers who provide care to the participating patients to be the study subjects to achieve a wider perspective → Purposive sampling, You want a systematic approach to analyse the data as and when it is collected. → Grounded theory


explanation:
Explanation:  Q1. To reach adequate sample size and stop collecting data, the point of theoretical saturation is employed in qualitative research. The data is iteratively analysed and at the point where no more new categories emerge, the data collection ceases. This point is called as theoretical saturation. Q2. Triangulation compares the results from either two or more different methods of data collection or two or more data sources. The researcher looks for patterns of convergence to develop or corroborate an overall interpretation. In investigator triangulation, more than one investigator is involved, and findings are cross-validated. Q3. Purposive sampling is one of the most common sampling strategies in qualitative research. (Note that snowball sampling and quota sampling are also used often). In purposive sampling the participants are selected according to a preselected criterion relevant to a particular research question - hence it is not random. "Sample sizes, which may or may not be fixed prior to data collection, depend on the resources and time available, as well as the study's objectives. Purposive sample sizes are often determined on the basis of theoretical saturation (the point in data collection when new data no longer bring additional insights to the research questions). Purposive sampling is, therefore, most successful when data review and analysis are done in conjunction with data collection"

(Retrieved from http://www.ccs.neu.edu/course/is4800sp12). Q4. Grounded theory refers to a constant comparison of the collected data alongside the data collection (iterative analysis).(Excerpt retrieved from Mays & Pope, BMJ 2000;320;50-52)

In 1946, Joseph Berkson highlighted that the relative frequency of disease in a group of patients who are hospitalised is inherently biased when compared to the population served by the hospital (Berkson Bias). This phenomenon is attributable to the way in which the probabilities of hospitalisation combine in patients with more than one disease (if you have two diseases, your probability of being hospitalised is greater than the probability associated with either disease separately). If, for example, obese people who have hypertension have a higher probability of being hospitalised than people with hypertension alone, a spurious association between obesity and anti- hypertensive drugs can be found. A late look at those exposed (or affected) early will miss fatal cases and short episodes, plus mild or silent cases and cases in which evidence of exposure disappears with disease onset. This is called as the Neyman bias or the prevalence-incidence bias. Diagnostic suspicion bias is described as the knowledge of the subject's prior exposure to a putative cause influencing both the intensity and the outcome of the diagnostic process. Sampling techniques for qualitative research A researcher wants to explore service users' perceptions and attitudes associated with the prescription and administration of clozapine in community mental health settings. He chooses to use one of the following sampling methods. Choose the correct term describing each approach from the list below.

The researcher chooses to offer a semi-structured interview to the patients who attend clozapine monitoring clinic once every three months. All active community clozapine users are registered to attend this clinic. Choose...

The researcher pursues a set of service users who experienced an unusual increase in sweating with clozapine. Another service user who shared the same effect introduced these patients to the researcher. Choose...

The researcher specifically attempts to include some highly satisfied service users, some poorly compliant users, and some users who discontinued early in the course and some users who continue to have psychotic Choose... symptoms despite high degree of concordance.

The researcher recruits four service-user experts who have wide experience of talking to clozapine users in the locality. Choose...


correctAnswer:
The researcher chooses to offer a semi-structured interview to the patients who attend clozapine monitoring clinic once every three months. All active community clozapine users are registered to attend this clinic. → Convenience sampling, The researcher pursues a set of service users who experienced an unusual increase in sweating with clozapine. Another service user who shared the same effect introduced these patients to the researcher. → Snowballing, The researcher specifically attempts to include some highly satisfied service users, some poorly compliant users, and some users who discontinued early in the course and some users who continue to have psychotic symptoms despite high degree of concordance. → Purposive sampling, The researcher recruits four service-user experts who have wide experience of talking to clozapine users in the locality. → Intensity sampling


explanation:
Convenience (or opportunistic) sampling is a technique that uses an open period of recruitment that continues until a set number of subjects, events, or institutions are enrolled. Here, the selection is based on a first-come, first-served basis. This approach is used in studies drawing on predefined populations such as participants in support groups or medical clinics. Second, purposive sampling is a practice where subjects are intentionally selected to represent some explicit predefined traits or conditions. This is analogous to stratified samples in probability-based approaches. The goal here is to provide for relatively equal numbers of different elements or people to enable exploration and description of the conditions and meanings occurring within each of the study conditions. The objective, however, is not to determine the prevalence, incidence, or causes. Third, snowballing or word-of-mouth techniques make use of participants as referral sources. Participants recommend others they know who may be eligible. Fourth, case study samples select a single individual, institution, or event as

the total sample. A variant is the key-informant approach or intensity sampling (Patton 1990) where a subject who is an expert in the topic of study serves to provide expert information on the specialized topic. When qualitative perspectives are sought as part of clinical or survey studies, the purposive or case study sampling techniques are generally the most useful.

explanation: The most popular economic evaluation method in health care is Cost effectiveness analysis. stem: In economic analysis which of the following represents the cost of pain and suffering from an intervention that cannot be quantified in monetary terms?
explanation: Indirect cost refers to the costs of an intervention that is not directly due to the intervention itself, but can be quantified in units other than currencies e.g. number of sick days off work when undertaking a hysterectomy. stem: A retrospective cohort study was used to measure inpatient service utilization in 63 consecutive treatment resistant schizophrenia patients started on clozapine from a geographical catchment area compared to a control group matched for previous inpatient service use. [Hayhurst KP et al. The cost-effectiveness of clozapine: a controlled, population-based, mirror-image study. Journal of Psychopharmacology 16(2) (2002) 169 –175]. Whose viewpoint has been used to measure the costs?
explanation: The costs were calculated based on factors such as bed days and hospitalisation costs. It was not based on the patient's loss of productivity or carer's costs, or societal burden. Thus, the computation has taken the viewpoint of hospital managers.

Medical students have unmet needs in the areas of career and wellness advising. A study was conducted to describe the development of an Advisory College Program (ACP) and assess its effectiveness compared to a traditional one-on-one faculty advisor system. The ACP, consisting of four colleges co-led by Advisory College Directors and supported by key Faculty, was developed to provide structured career and wellness advising. In the ACP programme, students had several impromptu meetings with advisors and took part in college-wide activities aimed at wellness and career counselling. The authors compared the ACP to the former Faculty Advisory Program (FAP, in which each medical student is paired with a volunteer faculty member who serves as the student's advisor) using two parallel questionnaires. The FAP survey was provided to second- and third-year medical students at the beginning of the academic year 2007 - 2008 and consisted of 53 items regarding their experiences with the FAP the previous year before the ACP programme began. The ACP survey was delivered to all first-year students at the end of the academic year 2007 -2008 and was based on their experiences with the ACP. Surveys were completed by 74% of first-year students, 60% of second-year students and 88% of third-year students. Survey data demonstrated a significant increase in the number of students who could identify their advisor, the frequency of student-advisor contacts, and the perceived accessibility of advisors in the ACP compared to the FAP. While an ordinal logistic regression model did not demonstrate a significant effect of the new advising system on overall satisfaction, univariate analysis demonstrated a significant increase in student satisfaction with wellness and career counseling. Based on the analysis of the single question "I am satisfied with the overall advisory system,'' there was a statistically significant improvement in the ACP compared to the FAP (67% vs. 24%; p<0.001; SA - Strongly Agree; SD - Strongly Disagree). The ACP was more effective in promoting student wellness and career counseling than the traditional one-on-one faculty advisor system. In this particular instance, the controls are historical (those who had exposure to the compared intervention at sometime in the past, not in parallel with the evaluated intervention). A simple before-and-after study is one in which there is only one group receiving the intervention, but their historical data before the intervention serves as the control arm for comparison. An extension of a simple before and after design is the interrupted time series study. As the name suggests, this design uses measurements obtained from multiple time points in a group before and after an intervention (or 'interruption'). The objective is to test whether the intervention has had any effect on the rate of improvement (or worsening, e.g. in dementia) seen in the group. Another variation is the controlled before-and-after study where outcome measures are assessed before and after the implementation of an intervention (usually a policy change or service-level intervention) not in one, but TWO groups with one group receiving the new intervention and the other (control) group undergoing before-after measurements with either no intervening intervention or after a placebo. http://ccg.cochrane.org/non-randomised-controlled-study-nrs-designs

stem: A researcher wants to make sure that the size of the control and two intervention groups are more or less equal so that statistical deductions can be meaningful. Which of the following methods of randomisation could ensure this?
explanation: Block randomization refers to a method where randomization occurs in a set of specified numbers, say blocks of 6 etc., to ensure equal number distribution between two arms. Larger the block size, lesser the ability to predict allocation. In cluster randomization, the unit of randomization and analysis is various centres or catchment-zones and not individual patients. Stratification is classifying to subgroups  before randomising within each subgroup to ensure impartial allocation of subgroup factors. Quasi-randomisation refers to 'randomizing' using even/odd numbers of the date of birth, day of the week patient was seen, etc.

stem: Which of the following is not a proper method of randomization?
options: Every 6 patients after recruitment are assigned according to a sequence; a new sequence is generated for the next 6.
Everyone with odd number of birth date gets treatment, even number gets placebo; the allocation takes place even before examining a
A random list generated by computer is used to assign groups
A random list generated using an excel sheet is administered by a third party
124 cities where a large RCT is planned are randomly allocated and every city allocated to one arm receives the same
correctAnswer:
Everyone with odd number of birth date gets treatment, even number gets placebo; the allocation takes place even before examining a patient.


explanation: Quasi-randomisation refers to randomizing using even/odd numbers of the date of birth, day of the week patient was seen, etc. These are not reproducible methods, and the sequences cannot ensure equal distribution of variables. These must be avoided. Computer generated  lists are commonly used and are acceptable. 'Six patient sequences' refer to block randomization. Randomization of cities refers to cluster randomization.

stem: To determine the efficacy of exposure therapy or cognitive restructuring relative to a wait-list control group in preventing chronic PTSD in those with acute stress reaction, a trial was designed. Participants were randomly allocated to 1 of 3 treatment conditions. Randomization was conducted by a process of stratification by sex, trauma type, and Acute Stress Disorder score. Random numbers system was administered by a third party in a distant centre not involved in the study. Which of the following is false with regard to the above study method?
options: All patients had equal chance of entering the waiting list group
An attempt has been made to conceal the random allcoation
Selection of patients who are less likely to develop PTSD to one group is avoided
Probability theory can be used to make inferences.
The baseline characters suspected to be important are randomly distributed
correctAnswer:
The baseline characters suspected to be important are randomly distributed


explanation:  The above design refers to RCT. So probability theory can be used (i.e. use of 'p-values'). Selection of a higher likelihood group to one side has been avoided by a process of stratification - so baseline characters are not truly random. This is preferred when the sample is small and will avoid skewed distribution of influential variables.

stem: To determine the efficacy of exposure therapy or cognitive restructuring relative to a wait-list control group in preventing chronic PTSD in those with acute stress reaction, a trial was designed. Participants were randomly allocated to 1 of 3 treatment conditions. Randomization was conducted by a process of stratification by sex, trauma type, and Acute Stress Disorder score. Random numbers system was administered by a third party in a distant centre not involved in the study. In the above study the reason for using a third party in assignment of random sequences is
options: To reduce the cost of the trial
To ensure subjects' compliance with intervention
explanation:  The reason for using a third party in the assignment of random sequences is to ensure allocation concealment. Allocation concealment refers to maintaining secrecy with regard to the allocation itself at the start of the study. Even if the study is randomized, at least one person in the trial team will have access to the generated random sequence and so can deduce where the next patient on the list will be allocated to. Concealing this information will avoid a selection bias wherein clinicians can pick up certain 'disease markers' that may make them favourably allocate a subject to one group or the other.

stem: Maintaining secrecy about the status of a patient as to which arm he or she belongs, once the allocation is complete is called
explanation: Blinding refers to maintaining secrecy about the status of a patient as to which arm he or she belongs, once the allocation is complete. If the participant only (or rarely therapist only) is not aware of what treatment he is receiving this is single blind. If both the participant and therapist are unaware, then this is double blind - this is the most common method. If the participant, therapist and the data analyzer - all three are unaware, this is called triple blind. If no one is blind, then it is called an open-label RCT. 

stem: Which of the following types of error is most obviously reduced by blinding in RCTs?
explanation: Blinding is necessary to obviate measurement bias - information bias, exposure suspicion/ascertainment bias (investigator having guessed who received the drug rather than placebo may unconsciously rate the improvement better).

stem: 100 patients are enrolled in an RCT comparing an herbal medicine with fluoxetine at 12 weeks for depression. Out of 50 who were assigned to take fluoxetine, 8 did not turn up for follow-up. Out of 50 who were assigned to herbal treatment, 12 did not complete the treatment or missing. Which of the following is the best way of reporting the results of this RCT?
options: Report the number improved out of 42 for fluoxetine and 38 for herbal medicine
Report the number improved out of 42 for fluoxetine and 50 for herbal medicine
Report the number improved out of 50 for fluoxetine and 38 for herbal medicine
This RCT should not be reported
Report the number improved out of 50 for fluoxetine and 50 for herbal medicine
correctAnswer:
Report the number improved out of 50 for fluoxetine and 50 for herbal medicine


explanation: The intention-to-treat principle holds that participants must be counted in the groups to which they were initially randomized, regardless of whether they were compliant with the allocated intervention. This includes participants who were withdrawn from active treatment for any  reason. This is the best way of reporting a trial result in most instances. So reporting the number improved out of 50 for fluoxetine and 50 for herbal medicine is preferable.

stem: 100 patients are enrolled in an RCT comparing an herbal medicine with fluoxetine at 12 weeks for depression. Out of 50 who were assigned to take fluoxetine, 8 did not turn up for follow-up. Out of 50 who were assigned to herbal treatment, 12 did not complete the treatment or missing. If the above study reports numbers improved out of all 100 randomised, which of the following processes has been carried out?
explanation: This is called intention to treat analysis. The rationale is that in most RCTs, one sets out to estimate the broader effects of allocating an intervention in clinical practice, rather than just the narrow effects in the subgroup of participants who adhere to it. The ITT strategy gives a  conservative estimate of the treatment effect compared with what would be expected in an ideal world of full compliance. Hence, ITT tends to make RCT results more generalizable and pragmatic.

stem: 100 patients are enrolled in an RCT comparing an herbal medicine with fluoxetine at 12 weeks for depression. Out of 50 who were assigned to take fluoxetine, 8 did not turn up for follow-up. Out of 50 who were assigned to herbal treatment, 12 did not complete the treatment or missing. In the above study in order to calculate the possible missing values of 20 patients, the statistician uses the HAMD score recorded at the most recent interview for the lost patients and includes them as the final score in analysis. This approach is called
explanation: This is called last observation carried forward LOCF method. There are many different ways by which one can substitute missing values  when doing (ITT) intention to treat analysis. The LOCF is only useful for longitudinal observations where continuous scales were used. E.g. in a clinical trial of fluoxetine for depression observed for six months, the 3rd month's HAMD/MADRS values can be carried forward to 4th, 5th and 6th months and used in the final analysis. But many psychiatric diseases have a natural course of remission. LOCF does not make allowances for this. LOCF is 'too good' for controls and 'too stringent' for the patient group.

stem: 100 patients are enrolled in an RCT comparing an herbal medicine with fluoxetine at 12 weeks for depression. Out of 50 who were assigned to take fluoxetine, 8 did not turn up for follow-up. Out of 50 who were assigned to herbal treatment 12 did not complete the treatment or missing. If such a trial is carried out to see the biological efficacy of the new herbal medicine and not to compare its clinical effectiveness against fluoxetine, which of the following methods of analysis will be most suitable?
explanation: ITT may not suit those who are investigating biological effects of a drug via RCT model - those who do not take the drug cannot have a  biological effect. But for those studies that report on effectiveness, ITT is invaluable. Using per-protocol (PP) analysis only patients who sufficiently complied with the trial's protocol are considered in the final analysis. This is the antithesis of intention to treat analysis. It is also called 'oeon treatment'' analysis. PP analysis is often carried out in biological explanatory RCTs and as the secondary analysis in effectiveness trials.

stem: Two educational interventions are compared with respect to efficacy in reducing psychosis related disability in high-risk individuals. The main outcome measured was median days of DUP (duration of untreated psychosis) reduced by each intervention. Which of the following is true concerning the above study method?
options: DUP is a secondary outcome measure
This study cannot be a randomised controlled trial
explanation: The researcher intends to demonstrate a reduction in psychosis related disability. But instead he/she chooses to measure median days of DUP, considering DUP as a proxy for disability related to psychosis. Hence, DUP is a surrogate endpoint. Secondary outcome measures are  outcomes from testing an additional hypothesis different from the primary one.

stem: In an allocation scheme, the next allocation of a subject depends on the characteristics of those already allocated. This scheme can be called
explanation: In minimisation schemes, next allocation depends on characteristics of those already allocated. Allocation of each participant aims to ensure a balance of prognostic factors between groups. The disadvantage is that this method is inferior to proper randomisation as it allocation is somewhat exposed and 'controlled' manually. 

stem: A single subject is administered placebo and active intervention in tandem under double-blind controlled conditions. This type of study could be called
explanation: N of 1 trial - here a single subject is administered placebo and active intervention (or two different interventions) in tandem under double- blind controlled conditions. This is the best way of optimizing a treatment schedule for an individual patient, but results cannot be generalized to other patients. 

stem: Which of the following factors seen in an RCT makes it different from natural clinical practice?
options: Frequent follow up and attention given to patients on trial
explanation: Some of the practices while conducting RCTs that alienate then from normal clinical practice are as follows: 1. Recruitment: from specialist centres 2. Patients with co-morbid medical or psychiatric disorders are excluded 3. Patients are carefully selected to generate homogeneous diagnostic groups 4. Patients are allocated the treatment at random (no negotiation during prescription) 5. Patients are given detailed information for informed consent (rare in clinical practice) 6. Placebo is used to compare active treatment 7. Patients are followed at  frequent intervals - often more frequent than clinical practice 8. Patients get detailed checklists of side-effects 9. Assessment end-point is typically 4-6 weeks 10. Often symptoms measures are the outcomes considered. 11. Patient and clinician are blind to treatment.

stem: As regards pragmatic trials:
options: It is essential to have modelled all the details of the intervention beforehand
The main aim is to tell us how well a drug works
They have more exclusive referral criteria than explanatory trials.
They are less generalisable than explanatory trials
explanation: Pragmatic trials are more practice-related and naturalistic than experimental RCTs. Certain variables such as strict exclusion/inclusion criteria, dose of the drug to be used, time at which change or switch occurs, etc. are not controlled as tightly as in RCTs. The main aim is to see how effective an intervention will be in clinical practice, rather than demonstrating the efficacy of a biological compound. They have higher external validity and are more generalisable. Tunis, SR et al. Practical clinical trials. JAMA, 2003. 290, 12, 1624 

stem: Concerning randomisation, choose the best option:
options: Non-randomised studies are less likely to be affected by confounding than randomised studies.
It can only be performed at the level of individual patients
It guarantees that the study will be free of confounders
It automatically leads to poor generalisability
Concealment of allocation of randomisation refers to whether the outcome of randomisation can be predicted
correctAnswer:
Concealment of allocation of randomisation refers to whether the outcome of randomisation can be predicted


explanation: Concealment of random allocation refers to whether the outcome of randomisation can be predicted or not. Randomisation can be done in clusters instead of individual patient units. Randomisation does not eliminate confounders fully; it only serves to eliminate their influence by equally distributing them across all groups. Randomisation is not always associated with poor generalisability; e.g. pragmatic RCTs are randomized but still have good generalisability. Altman DG and Schulz KF. Concealing treatment allocation in randomized trials. BMJ  2001;323:446-447

stem: Which of the following is correct with respect to sample size in research studies?
options: We do not need to randomize if our sample size is sufficiently large
A larger sample size is needed only for a larger population
A large sample size ensures representativeness of the sample
Irrespective of size, proper sampling techniques will ensure precision of estimates.
correctAnswer:
A large sample size ensures representativeness of the sample


explanation: The necessity for randomisation does not depend on sample size, but in very small samples randomisation is difficult and can become meaningless. Irrespective of population size, a large sample size ensures representativeness to a certain degree. Precision is very much dependent on number of observations i.e. sample size. It is not ensured by mere randomisation. 

stem: An RCT was terminated following an interim analysis as it was deemed unfair to continue placebo for one group of trial participants as the active arm showed huge beneficial effect. Which of the following is the likely problem with this practice of stopping trials earlier due to the observation of apparently large benefit?
options: Ethically unacceptable to stop RCTs midway
Higher rates of attrition may occur
Intention to treat analysis may not be possible
explanation: Taking the point estimate of the treatment effect at face value may overestimate the actual effect if the trial is stopped early due to apparently high benefit. The smaller the number of events, the greater the risk that the play of chance will result in apparent effects far from  the truth. If these studies are allowed to continue longer, the random high of treatment effects may even out. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg 154

stem: In the traditional hierarchy of evidence in EBM for therapy, which of the following occupies the highest level
explanation: The generally agreed-upon hierarchies of evidence indicate that certain types of research results should be given more weight than other types. The specific hierarchy depends on the type of clinical question being asked. Results from a systematic review of RCTs should be given more weight than the results of a single RCT, and results from an RCT should be given more weight than results from uncontrolled or nonexperimental studies. 

stem: A published study reported the use of prospective data collected to compare the effectiveness and tolerability of divalproex and valproic acid in 9,260 psychiatric admissions. All participating clinicians were allowed to initiate treatment with either valproic acid or divalproex and switch medications without restrictions, on the basis of what they believed to be in the patients' best interest. This study is best described as
explanation: A quasi-experiment is often used in the social sciences. ("Quasi" stands for likeness or resembling) Quasi-experiments share characteristics of true experiments that seek interventions or treatments. The key difference in this empirical approach is the lack of random assignment.  In contrast, pragmatic RCTs are randomised.

stem: In an adequately randomized, well-concealed RCT evaluating the efficacy of depot risperidone against oral risperidone, the participants receiving oral risperidone were reviewed every four weeks in the clinic. The participants receiving depot were seen by community nurse every two weeks who administered the depot. The drop-out rates were comparable, and the outcomes were measured by involved clinicians using standardised tools. The result strongly favoured the use of the depot. Which one of the following bias is most likely to have occurred?
explanation:  Blinding is an attempt to prevent observer bias. If an interviewer or rater knows which treatment a patient is receiving, he or she may differentially inquire about certain symptoms or see improvement where none exists. Gray GE. Evidence-based psychiatry. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2004.Pg 58

stem: Which of the following group involved in an RCT must be blind to treatment in order to avoid bias due to cointervention?
explanation: A clinician involved in a trial providing additional care (e.g., time, support, etc.) to patients in one treatment group but not to those in the other treatment group leads to cointervention or performance bias. In clinical trials, this effect can be minimized by blinding clinicians to the treatment being provided. Gray GE. Evidence-based psychiatry. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2004.Pg 57 

stem: In a treatment trial that favoured active intervention against placebo, high number of subjects are lost to follow-up. Which of the following would reassure you that the validity of study results is not affected badly by the high attrition?
options: Best case scenario assumption does not change the inferences
Less than 20% are lost to follow up
The sample size is larger than 300
There is comparable loss on both arms of the trial
Worst case scenario assumption does not change the inferences
correctAnswer:
Worst case scenario assumption does not change the inferences


explanation: One of the major sources of bias in cohort studies/RCTs concerns patients lost to follow-up. If patients lost to follow-up differ in outcomes from patients who remain in the study, estimates will be biased. This is called migration bias or attrition bias. One way of dealing with losses to follow-up in the analysis is to perform a best case/worst case analysis, a form of sensitivity analysis in which outcome statistics are first  calculated assuming all of those lost to follow-up did well, then recalculated assuming all of those lost to follow-up had a bad outcome. A positive treatment trial that favours intervention, if withstands worst case assumption, then one can be reassured that the direction of results cannot be influenced by lost patients.

stem: In which of the following studies a qualitative approach is most appropriate?
options: A comparison of the effectiveness of tetrabenazine vs. reserpine in the treatment of tardive dyskinesia.
A survey of number of school teachers exposed to bullying from students and the distribution of mental health problems among those
A multicenter pragmatic naturalistic exploration of all cause discontinuation rates for antidepressants.
An exploration of the role of the 'Community team coordinators' in the elderly community health care teams in the North East of
A national postal survey of doctor's knowledge of prescribing nicotine replacement therapies.
correctAnswer:
An exploration of the role of the 'Community team coordinators' in the elderly community health care teams in the North East of England.

explanation: Tetrabenazine trial is clearly quantitative. National surveys of knowledge and practice are usually conducted through questionnaires which collect feeble qualitative information; these are analysed quantitatively on most occasions. The last example is a pragmatic RCT, far from a  qualitative study. Some situations where qualitative research is useful are, 1. stem: Which of the following is generally a feature of qualitative but not quantitative research?
explanation: Testing a hypothesis, random sampling, controlled interventions or exploration of aetiology and generalising inferences (deductive approach) are used in quantitative research. Qualitative research uses a purposeful sample, often includes outliers and anomalies, in order to generate a theory or hypothesis. 

stem: In grounded theory method of qualitative research, the term theoretical saturation is used to describe which of the following?
options: Point at which the research hypothesis is fully formed
Point at which the research is stopped
Point at which no new categories can be developed from the available data
Process of checking validity of information using various sources of data
Process of testing new categories using fresh data
correctAnswer:
Point at which no new categories can be developed from the available data


explanation: The grounded theory refers to a technique of generating theories/categories using qualitative methods. In this technique, i. Initially, a constant comparison of the collected data takes place in different stages of the data collection. ii. From these comparisons, categories are generated until nothing new is revealed, i.e. the point of theoretical saturation is reached. iii. Later these categories are tested by collecting further fresh data on the basis of the new categories made - this is called theoretical sampling. 

stem: Which of the following methods is the most appropriate to explore the experience and meaning of stigma by schizophrenia patients, their relatives, and health professionals?
options: A case control study with two control groups
A well constructed single self report questionnaire
Participant observation for all three groups individually
Postal survey with rewards for returning the questionnaire
explanation: Conducting interviews in a group format with some predetermined structure for such groups, in order to provide a focus for discussion, is called 'focus groups' (Kitzinger, 1995). Focus groups usually contain a small number of members selected giving views on the chosen topic; the discussion here is semi-structured guided by key points. These are useful in gathering opinions of service users and providers. Postal  surveys and self-report questionnaires do not generate much data needed for adequate understanding of 'life experiences'.

stem: In which of the following research methods the clear cut demarcation between researcher" and "researched" may not be so apparent?"
explanation: PAR (or simply action research) involves individuals and groups researching their own personal beings, socio-cultural settings and experiences. The clear cut demarcation between and 'researcher' and the 'researched' that is found in other types of research may not be so apparent in action research. For example, a PAR study may involve researchers working with carers of schizophrenia patients to identify which family or environmental situations provide substantial challenges to the service users. Meyer, J. (2000) Qualitative research in health  care. Using qualitative methods in health related action research. British Medical Journal, 320, 178-181

stem: In a research interview, the interviewer does not follow any order but frames the questions on the basis of the interviewee's previous response. Which of the following style is he following?
explanation: In structured interviews, a tight schedule of questions may be used with an intention to elicit one of the few limited range of responses, similar to a questionnaire. Semi-structured interviews (sometimes referred to as focused interviews) involve a series of open-ended questions based on the topic areas the researcher wants to cover. Though there is a schedule of topics to cover, the exact way questions are  phrased is not premeditated or dictated by a list. Unstructured interviews are also referred to as 'in-depth' interviews where the interviewer has some limited number of topics in his mind but does not follow any order and frames the questions on the basis of the interviewee's previous response

stem: A researcher organises focus groups to explore the experience of being admitted to an intensive psychiatric care ward. All of the following will increase the usefulness of the study method except
options: More than one focus group is used in the actual project
Having a good degree of group interaction
Having a predetermined topic to discuss at the group
All members of the groups have the common experience of being inpatients in the ward
Each group has around 24 to 36 subjects only
correctAnswer:
Each group has around 24 to 36 subjects only


explanation: Focus groups are very useful when limited resources prevent individual interviews. They are used when the studied individuals share a common factor where collecting views of several of them may be useful; these factors should be important to the topic of investigation. If group interaction may allow greater insights to be developed, focus groups may be used. Members must be usually 6 - 10; it is not a good  idea to have just one group for the whole research - many small groups must be included in the research

stem: Which of the following terms describe the procedure for producing a written version of a qualitative research interview?
explanation: Data collection process in qualitative research includes transcribing. Transcribing is the procedure for producing a written version of the interview. stem: In qualitative studies, semi-structured interviews are often chosen over other forms of interviews. This is because
options: Good balance between resource limitations and amount of data collected
Easy accessibility of established interview schedules
correctAnswer:
Good balance between resource limitations and amount of data collected


explanation: The strengths of the semistructured interview methodology include its ability to balance the need for acquiring good quality data that is required to investigate complex behaviors and motivations with the limited time available to researchers in the field. In addition, semi- structured interviews have better response rates than a questionnaire survey; are particularly useful when discussing sensitive issues as they enable the researcher to explore new phenomenon as well as enquire about expected phenomena; achieve good comparability by  ensuring that all items are answered by each participant; ensure that the responses are not influenced by group dynamics or assistance from others; are more informative when there are large variations within the sample groups, regardless of the factors that bring about those variations. In the presence of such variability, a structured interview might not pick the underlying differences while an unstructured interview may lose focus and fail to answer the primary research question. Leech, B. (2002). Asking questions: Techniques for semistructured interviews. Political Science and Politics. 35(4):665-668.

stem: Woolf et al., BMJ 2008; 337. 27 year 3 medical students and 25 clinical teachers at a London medical school, selected for required ethnicity and sex, participated in a study that used semistructured one to one interviews and focus groups. Ethnic stereotypes of UK medical students were explored in the context of academic underachievement of medical students from ethnic minorities. Overall, 26 of 40 clinical teachers agreed to be interviewed (65%), 12 did not answer, and two declined: one was too busy and one did not give a reason. Of the 49 students invited to participate, 21 agreed to be interviewed (43%). Twelve interviews took place—six with white students and six with students from ethnic minorities. correctAnswer: Approaches to ensure quality and safety of health services
explanation: Quality Improvement is a scientific approach to tackle the challenge of ensuring quality and safety of healthcare provision. QI method includes both systematic analysis of performance and interventions to improve it.

stem: Which of the following differentiates a quality improvement project from a research project?

Interventions tested in Quality Improvement projects are not novel
correctAnswer: Interventions tested in Quality Improvement projects are not novel
explanation: It is important to note that QI projects are fundamentally similar to scientific research projects in health care. PDSA involves prediction of the outcome of a test of change (hypothesis statement) and subsequent measurement over time (quantitative or qualitative measurement) to assess the impact of an intervention (experimental manipulation) on the process or outcomes of interest. But in QI projects, the tested interventions are within established standards of care. 

stem: Which of the following provides a method for structuring iterative development of change as part of wider quality improvement approaches in health services?
explanation: PDSA is often the central component of QI initiatives. PDSA stands for Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle. Most often in healthcare, ideas are introduced top-down without adequate evaluation. PDSA cycles provide means to integrate top-down ideas with bottom-up observations before implementation. PDSA allows us to test an idea by temporarily trialling a change and assessing its impact. The PDSA method  originates from quality improvement studies in the industry. Shewhart and Deming initially described iterative processes that eventually became known as the four stages of PDSA.

stem: Which of the following methods of quality improvement focuses only on retrospective evaluation?
explanation: Root cause analysis (RCA) is a well-established QI method, though some argue that it is mostly a Quality Assurance process that QI. RCA involves a retrospective investigation that occurs after a sentinel event (usually an adverse event e.g. an inpatient suicide). RCA aims to identify the putative fundamental reasons (casual factors) explaining variation in performance that resulted in the sentinel event. RCA focusses on individual events and suffers from hindsight bias, wherein findings may apply only to the specific event and not to the system as  a whole

stem: Which of the following methods of quality improvement is based on 80/20 rule of management?
explanation: A Pareto chart is nothing but a bar chart but the bars are reorganised to show the categories with most frequent showing events on the left and the least frequent to the right. Sometimes a line showing cumulative frequency is also superimposed. A Pareto chart helps us to visualise the high-yield events, which when focussed upon, can result in maximum improvement. (This charting follows the 80/20 economic principle. 80% of the income of a nation generally goes only to 20% of the population. By focusing on the 20% of high-impact circumstances,  nearly 80% of problems can be managed).

stem: Which of the following refers to Quality Improvement activity?

explanation: Quality Improvement involves both prospective and retrospective evaluation strategies that are aimed at improvement. QI specifically focuses on determining 'what will work better', avoiding blame attribution, and to create systems to prevent rather than rectify errors.

explanation: Narrative reviews are usually carried out by experts in the field of study and are more or less close to an expert's opinion supported by research evidence.
